AMI Program Implementation Assessment

Water-use analysis, anomaly detection, and conservation targeting

Prepared with R + Snowflake

May 29, 2026

Executive summary

This assessment demonstrates an end-to-end Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) analysis workflow built in R on data managed in Snowflake. It processes hourly interval reads to (1) characterize water-use patterns, (2) automatically flag anomalies such as leaks and meter errors, (3) segment customers for targeted conservation, and (4) quantify non-revenue water (NRW).

Dataset at a glance
Metric Value
Meters analyzed 60
Hourly interval reads 129,600
Period 2025-04-01 to 2025-06-29
Total metered volume (gal) 4,751,289

Note on data. This report runs on a realistic synthetic AMI dataset so it is fully reproducible without exposing client data. The identical workflow reads from a live Snowflake warehouse when credentials are configured (source = "snowflake"). See README.md for the data dictionary and the Snowflake DDL in sql/.

1. Water-use patterns

System-wide daily demand

Diurnal profile by customer class

Different customer classes have distinct daily signatures. Residential demand is twin-peaked (morning and evening); commercial accounts plateau through business hours; irrigation concentrates in pre-dawn and evening watering windows. These shapes drive both demand forecasting and anomaly baselines.

2. Anomaly detection

We run four transparent, parameterized detectors over the interval reads. Each is designed to be replicable across clients by adjusting thresholds:

Detector Signal Typical cause
Leak Sustained step-up in overnight minimum flow (net of seasonal growth) Underground/service-line leak, stuck fixture
Continuous use Meter essentially never reads zero Running toilet, stuck valve, process load
Stuck meter Long run of identical/zero reads Register failure, lost AMI comms, vacancy
Meter error Negative or physically impossible reads Register rollover, AMI decode error

Detector validation

Because the synthetic data carries known ground-truth anomalies, we can score the detectors directly — evidence the methods actually work rather than just producing plausible-looking output.

3. Customer segmentation

Behavioural features (peakiness, overnight share, weekday/weekend ratio, seasonal sensitivity) classify customers independent of their billing class — portable across utilities. We show a transparent rule-based tiering plus an unsupervised k-means discovery view.

4. Non-revenue water (NRW)

NRW is the gap between water supplied into the system and water metered to customers — a key efficiency and loss-control metric.

5. Recommendations

Typical roadmap actions an analyst would draw from these results:

  1. Dispatch leak investigations to the top-ranked overnight-flow meters, starting with the highest estimated wasted volume.
  2. Customer outreach to continuous-use and high-overnight accounts (often a running toilet — a low-cost, high-impact fix).
  3. Data-quality remediation for meters reporting negative/stuck reads before they corrupt billing and downstream analytics.
  4. Targeted conservation to “Very High” tier and irrigation-driven segments, where per-account savings potential is largest.
  5. Track NRW against the dashed baseline; sustained increases warrant a district-metered-area (DMA) loss audit.

Reproduce this report: run R/01_generate_synthetic_ami.R then knit this file (rmarkdown::render("reports/ami_assessment.Rmd")), or point it at Snowflake by configuring config.yml and setting SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD.
